nodes.label: Gravitation
nodes.note: Newtonian gravity from the inverse-square law through fields, potentials, energy, Kepler orbits, and satellites. Reduce every question to a force balance, an energy equation, or a potential gradient.

nodes.label: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
nodes.note: Central inverse-square attraction between any two masses, plus its vector and superposition forms. All gravitational problems begin here.

nodes.label: Statement of the Law
nodes.note: Every pair of point masses attracts with $$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$, where $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{/kg}^2$ is universal. The force is independent of the medium between the masses.

nodes.label: Vector Formulation
nodes.note: The force lies along the line joining the masses: $$\vec{F}_{12} = -G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^3}\vec{r}_{12}$$. Action and reaction are equal and opposite, so the pair conserves momentum.

nodes.label: Superposition Principle
nodes.note: The net force on a test mass is the vector sum of pairwise forces: $$\vec{F} = \sum_i -G\frac{m_0 m_i}{r_i^3}\vec{r}_i$$. A third mass never alters the interaction between two given masses.

nodes.label: Shell Theorem
nodes.note: A uniform spherical shell attracts an exterior mass as if all its mass were at the centre, and exerts no net force on an interior mass: $$E_{out} = -\frac{GM}{r^2},\quad E_{in} = 0$$. This legitimises treating planets as point masses externally.

nodes.label: Inside the Shell
nodes.note: Every interior point has zero field and constant potential: $$E = 0,\quad V = -\frac{GM}{R}$$. Gravity cannot be used to localise mass inside a hollow shell.

nodes.label: Outside the Shell
nodes.note: For $r \ge R$ the field and potential match those of a point mass $M$ at the centre: $$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$$. The potential is continuous across the surface.

nodes.label: Gravitational Field and Potential
nodes.note: Field intensity, potential, and their gradients for standard mass distributions. Circular reasoning between E and V is what JEE exploits.

nodes.label: Field Intensity
nodes.note: Field intensity is force per unit test mass: $$\vec{E} = -\frac{GM}{r^2}\hat{r}$$. Numerically it equals $\vec{g}$ at the same point, in N/kg or m/s$^2$.

nodes.label: Gravitational Potential
nodes.note: Potential is work per unit mass brought slowly from infinity: $$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$$. It is negative everywhere because gravity is purely attractive and $V(\infty) = 0$.

nodes.label: Field from Potential Gradient
nodes.note: The field is the negative gradient of potential: $$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$$. Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines.

nodes.label: Ring on Its Axis
nodes.note: For a ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$, an axial point at $x$ sees $$V = -\frac{GM}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$$. The axial field peaks at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$ and vanishes at the centre.

nodes.label: Solid Sphere: Interior Field
nodes.note: Only the enclosed mass matters inside a uniform sphere: $$E = \frac{G M r}{R^3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi G \rho\, r$$. Hence $E$ grows linearly from zero at the centre.

nodes.label: Potential at the Centre
nodes.note: Integrating the interior field gives $$V_{center} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{GM}{R} = \frac{3}{2}V_{surface}$$. It is the deepest (most negative) point of the sphere.

nodes.label: Neutral Point Between Two Masses
nodes.note: Between two attracting masses there is one point of zero field: $$\frac{M_1}{x^2} = \frac{M_2}{(D - x)^2} \Rightarrow x = \frac{\sqrt{M_1}}{\sqrt{M_1} + \sqrt{M_2}}D$$. Potential there is negative and is never a maximum of force.

nodes.label: Variation of g
nodes.note: How the measured value of g shifts with altitude, depth, latitude, and planetary shape. Sign errors in these approximations are a classic trap.

nodes.label: Altitude Dependence
nodes.note: Above the surface gravity falls as $$g_h = \frac{g}{(1 + h/R)^2} \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$$ for $h \ll R$. The fractional drop is $2h/R$.

nodes.label: Depth Dependence
nodes.note: Below the surface only the inner sphere pulls, so $$g_d = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$$, falling linearly to zero at the centre. A depth of $d = 2h$ matches the gravity loss at height $h$.

nodes.label: Rotation and Latitude
nodes.note: Centrifugal effect of spin reduces effective gravity: $$g_{eff} = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\theta$$. The reduction is maximal at the equator and zero at the poles.

nodes.label: Shape of the Earth
nodes.note: The oblate earth has $R_{eq} > R_{pole}$, and since $$g \propto \frac{1}{R^2}$$, polar gravity exceeds equatorial gravity. Combined with rotation, $g_{pole} - g_{eq} \approx 0.034\ \text{m/s}^2$.

nodes.label: Altitude vs Depth Rate
nodes.note: Differentiating the two approximations gives $$\left|\frac{dg_h}{dh}\right| = \frac{2g}{R} = 2\left|\frac{dg_d}{dd}\right|$$. Gravity weakens twice as fast with height as with depth.

nodes.label: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: Energetics of assemblies of masses and the minimum speed needed to leave a planet forever. Energy bookkeeping replaces force bookkeeping here.

nodes.label: Two-Body Potential Energy
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: The mutual potential energy of masses $M$ and $m$ is $$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$$. Lifting a body by $h$ from the surface costs $$\Delta U = \frac{mgh}{1 + h/R} \approx mgh$$ for $h \ll R$.

nodes.label: Gravitational Self-Energy
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: The work to assemble a uniform sphere from dispersed matter is $$U_{self} = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R}$$, while a thin shell needs $$-\frac{GM^2}{2R}$$. Self-energy sets the magnitude of binding in stars and planets.

nodes.label: Escape Speed
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: Zero total energy at infinity defines the escape speed: $$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2\ \text{km/s}$$. It is independent of projectile mass and launch direction unless the path intersects the planet.

nodes.label: Escape Variants
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: From height $h$ or at speed boosted at some point, use energy conservation with $$\frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{GM}{r} = const$$. On the Moon $v_e \approx 2.4\ \text{km/s}$, explaining its airless surface.

nodes.label: Kepler's Laws
nodes.note: The three empirical laws of planetary motion, all derivable from Newtonian gravity. Expect one derivation-based question every year.

nodes.label: First Law: Orbits
nodes.note: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus: $$a = \frac{r_p + r_a}{2},\quad r_p = a(1 - e),\quad r_a = a(1 + e)$$. The semi-major axis $a$ alone fixes the energy of the orbit.

nodes.label: Second Law: Equal Areas
nodes.note: Areal velocity is constant because angular momentum is conserved: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m} = \frac{1}{2}r^2\omega = const$$. Hence planets move fastest at perihelion: $$\frac{v_p}{v_a} = \frac{r_a}{r_p}$$.

nodes.label: Third Law: Harmonic Law
nodes.note: The period squared scales with the cube of the semi-major axis: $$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$$. For two planets around the same star, $T_1^2/T_2^2 = a_1^3/a_2^3$.

nodes.label: Satellite Motion
nodes.note: Circular orbits, orbital energy, geostationary and polar satellites, and classification by launch speed. Pure centripetal-gravity balance.

nodes.label: Orbital Speed
nodes.note: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $$\frac{mv_0^2}{r} = \frac{GMm}{r^2} \Rightarrow v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$. A near-Earth satellite needs $v_0 \approx 7.9\ \text{km/s}$.

nodes.label: Orbital Period
nodes.note: The period follows from $T = 2\pi r/v_0$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(R + h)^3}{GM}}$$. A near-Earth orbit takes about $84$ minutes.

nodes.label: Satellite Energy
nodes.note: Summing kinetic and potential terms gives a negative total: $$E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -K = \frac{U}{2}$$. The binding energy that must be supplied to free the satellite is $|E|$.

nodes.label: Binding Energy
nodes.note: Binding energy equals the energy needed to reach infinity with zero speed: $$BE = \frac{GMm}{2r}$$. It grows as the orbit shrinks, so low orbits are more tightly bound.

nodes.label: Geostationary Satellite
nodes.note: A geostationary orbit matches Earth's spin: $T = 86400\ \text{s}$, equatorial plane, prograde motion. Its radius is $$r = \left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} \approx 6.6 R \Rightarrow h \approx 36000\ \text{km}$$.

nodes.label: Trajectory vs Launch Speed
nodes.note: Launch speed selects the conic: $v < v_0$ sub-orbital ellipse, $v = v_0$ circle, $v_0 < v < v_e$ ellipse, $v = v_e$ parabola, $v > v_e$ hyperbola. Only the last two escape: $$v_{\infty} = \sqrt{v^2 - v_e^2}$$.

nodes.label: Binary Star Systems
nodes.note: Two stars orbiting their common centre of mass, reducible to a one-body problem via reduced mass. A direct application of Kepler's third law.

nodes.label: Centre of Mass
nodes.note: Both stars circle the common CM with $$m_1 r_1 = m_2 r_2,\quad r_1 + r_2 = d$$. The lighter star moves on the larger orbit.

nodes.label: Reduced Mass
nodes.note: The two-body motion is equivalent to one body of mass $$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$$ orbiting a fixed centre. All one-body formulas apply with $\mu$ in place of $m$.

nodes.label: Period of the Binary
nodes.note: Balancing gravity against centripetal force for each star gives $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{G(m_1 + m_2)}}$$. Kinetic energies split inversely with mass: $K_1/K_2 = m_2/m_1$.
